newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. refugee chief visits Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. refugee chief visits Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for refugees, Sadako Ogata, arrived in Zaire on Friday as fighting escalated in the country's east, trapping hundreds of thousands of refugees in the war zone.
Ogata, who has called for a political and security solution to the Tutsi-led revolt in east Zaire, was due to meet the Zairean authorities and aid agency representatives, relief officials said.
The rebels, who hold towns and territory in the east, have pushed west over the past few days despite a January 20 army counter-offensive.
But military officials in Kinshasa said on Friday that the army had hit back, recapturing the towns of Watsa and Shabunda and inflicting serious losses on the Tutsi-led rebels.

A senior defence official and sources at army headquarters in Kinshasa said the Zairean armed forces had bombarded rebel positions from the air around the town of Walikale, which the army says it holds.

"The fighting at Watsa was extremely heavy. But we took them by surprise and Watsa was completely retaken overnight. There were 800 rebels killed," the official said, adding that nine prisoners had been taken and six tanks captured.
He said Shabunda, which fell to rebels on Wednesday, had been recaptured on Thursday.

Church sources in the region said on Wednesday that many of the rebels, who launched their revolt in October, had passed through Shabunda and were heading in the direction of Kindu, where the army concentrated troops for its counter-offensive.
There was no independent confirmation of the recapture of the towns but independent sources in the region confirmed that Walikale had been bombarded from the air on Thursday.
"In the surrounding areas around Walikale there were heavy bombardments to clean up all pockets of resistance," the senior defence official said.
Rwandan Hutu refugee camps along the road from Walikale to Kisangani, headquarters for the Zairean counter-offensive, were tense on Friday, aid workers said.
They reported 70 wounded soldiers arriving at Lubutu hospital, about 200 km (125 miles) from Kisangani.
Relief groups evacuated non-essential staff from Lubutu on Friday and made contingency plans to evacuate remaining staff should the situation continue to deteriorate.
But the World Food Programme in Nairobi said Zairean troops had stopped six local aid workers leaving and mistreated them.
Ogata was due to visit the nearby refugee camp at Tingi Tingi on Saturday.
The U.N. Children's Fund (UNICEF) estimated that 772 of the 120,000 refugees there have died from hunger or disease there since February 3. More than 400 were children under five.
Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 but bowed to pressure for democratic reform in 1990, was expected back home by the weekend after tests in Europe following prostate surgery in August.
On his way back, he visited Morocco, which sent troops to help him crush rebellions in Shaba in the 1970s. Before leaving Rabat on Friday, he denied he had gone to seek military help.
